For example, 

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

Let's evaluate this integral in this case where $C$ is given by the line segment

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].
$$

Along the path $C,$ we have

$$
x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.
$$

Computing the derivative of $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,j \\  & =6\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x+(x-y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t+1+2t+1)\cdot 6+(6t+1-(2t+1))\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\cdot 6+(4t)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}48t+12+8t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}56t+12\,\text{d}t \\  & ={28{t}^{2}+12t|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =28+12 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7c3e84f3-cbc8-5522-87f2-5accaa3854e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4437 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "621fd314-933c-56a6-97f4-7a591c8ceee3" :step/math-academy-id 27289 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180394}} {:db/id 17592186180476 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179729 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179591 :question/id #uuid "2b0b2d1f-df55-56cf-9ae9-ccef499e2352" :question/math-academy-id "e-9517"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1b5ecc45-95ec-55c0-86bf-bbaeffef4049" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180014} {:db/id 17592186180176} {:db/id 17592186259741} {:db/id 17592186259742} {:db/id 17592186259744} {:db/id 17592186259746} {:db/id 17592186387574} {:db/id 17592186387581} {:db/id 17592186387588}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z"} :step/id #uuid "3d3c67b4-ef9a-5648-81cf-8ed48d14fa68" :step/math-academy-id 35620 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180487}} {:db/id 17592186180477 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180712 :tutorial/content "Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function of three variables and $C$ be a path in three-dimensional space. $$

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy +   f \, \textrm dz
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

$$
\int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} +   f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

$$
\int_a^b f x'+ f y' +   f z' \,\textrm d t,
$$

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].
$$

Along the path $C,$ we have

$$
